questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Natural Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=ln⁡u,\,u=9x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=9.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 9 \\  & =\frac{1}{9x}\cdot 9 \\  & =\frac{9}{9x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{9}}{\cancel{9}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Natural Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=ln⁡u,\,u=7-4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{7-4x}\cdot (-4) \\  & =-\frac{4}{7-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=-1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=-1} & ={-\frac{4}{7-4x}|}_{x=-1} \\  & =-\frac{4}{7-4(-1)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{11}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $f(x)=4ln⁡(2x)$ at the point $(4,4ln⁡8).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=4ln⁡u,\,u=2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{4}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{4}{u}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{4}{2x}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{8}{2x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{2}\cdot 4}{\cancel{2}\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{4}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=4$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=4} & ={\frac{4}{x}|}_{x=4}=\frac{4}{4}=1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(4,4ln⁡8)$ is $m=1.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4ln⁡(8) & =1(x-4) \\ y & =x-4+4ln⁡(8)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=ln⁡u,\,u=5{x}^{2}+4.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 10x \\  & =\frac{1}{5{x}^{2}+4}\cdot 10x \\  & =\frac{10x}{5{x}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1} & ={\frac{10x}{5{x}^{2}+4}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{10(1)}{5({1}^{2})+4} \\  & =\frac{10}{9}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a General Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={log}_{3}⁡(5x-2)+5$ at the point where $x=\frac{7}{15}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{3}⁡(u)+5,\,u=5x-2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(3)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(3)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{1}{(5x-2)ln⁡(3)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{5}{(5x-2)ln⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=\frac{7}{15}$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=7/15} & =\frac{5}{(5x-2)ln⁡(3)}{|}_{x=7/15} \\  & =\frac{5}{(5(\frac{7}{15})-2)ln⁡(3)} \\  & =\frac{5}{\frac{1}{3}ln⁡(3)} \\  & =\frac{15}{ln⁡(3)}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{6}⁡(u),\,u=-3{x}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(6)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-9{x}^{2}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(6)}\cdot (-9{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{-9{x}^{2}}{-3{x}^{3}ln⁡(6)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{-3{x}^{2}}\cdot 3}{\cancel{-3{x}^{2}}\cdot xln⁡(6)} \\  & =\frac{3}{xln⁡(6)}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{3}⁡(u),\,u=\sqrt{2x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(3)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{x}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x}}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$

$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{4}⁡(u)+7,\,u=6x-2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{uln⁡(4)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{uln⁡(4)}\cdot 6 \\  & =\frac{1}{(6x-2)ln⁡(4)}\cdot 6 \\  & =\frac{6}{(6x-2)ln⁡(4)} \\  & =\frac{3}{(3x-1)ln⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1} & =\frac{3}{(3x-1)ln⁡(4)}{|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{3}{(3(1)-1)ln⁡(4)} \\  & =\frac{3}{2ln⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Natural Logarithm Function Using the Chain Rule
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = \ln u, \qquad u = x^2-4.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = \dfrac{1}{u},\qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = 2x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-4}\cdot 2x \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}-4}.\end{aligned}
$$
